title: Hatred is not settled by hatred
situation: A man has been wronged by a neighbour and is deciding how to answer it.
wise_response: The verse says hatred is never settled by hatred, only by its absence: this is the ancient teaching.
why_it_worked: It breaks the exchange at the point where it would otherwise repeat, so the wrong stops with him instead of passing to the next round.
tempting_wrong_answer: Answer the wrong with an equal wrong, and call it justice.
original_text: Na hi verena verāni, sammantīdha kudācanaṁ; Averena ca sammanti, esa dhammo sanantano.
scholarly_translation: For never is hatred laid to rest by hate, it's laid to rest by love: this is an ancient teaching.

title: The one who understands restrains himself
situation: Two groups are quarrelling, and a man can see clearly who is at fault.
wise_response: The verse says that those who understand should restrain themselves, because that is how quarrels are settled.
why_it_worked: Being right is not the same as being useful. The one who understands can end the conflict by not adding to it.
tempting_wrong_answer: Say the true thing at full force, since being right is enough.
original_text: Pare ca na vijānanti, mayamettha yamāmase; Ye ca tattha vijānanti, tato sammanti medhagā.
scholarly_translation: When others do not understand, let us, who do understand this, restrain ourselves in this regard; for that is how conflicts are laid to rest.

title: Praise and blame do not move the wise
situation: A man is praised in public one week and blamed in public the next.
wise_response: The verse compares the wise to a solid rock: the wind does not move it, and neither praise nor blame moves them.
why_it_worked: If neither report changes his course, he can act on what he judged before the reports came.
tempting_wrong_answer: Adjust his position to whatever the room currently approves.
original_text: Selo yathā ekaghano, vātena na samīrati; Evaṁ nindāpasaṁsāsu, na samiñjanti paṇḍitā.
scholarly_translation: As the wind cannot stir a solid mass of rock, so too blame and praise do not affect the wise.

title: Better to conquer oneself
situation: A man has spent years trying to outdo other people and is exhausted.
wise_response: The verse says conquering oneself is better than conquering everyone else, and praises the one who is tamed and lives restrained.
why_it_worked: It moves the contest to the only opponent he can actually train, so the effort produces something instead of only consuming him.
tempting_wrong_answer: Keep measuring himself against the next rival.
original_text: Attā have jitaṁ seyyo, yā cāyaṁ itarā pajā; Attadantassa posassa, niccaṁ saññatacārino.
scholarly_translation: It is surely better to conquer oneself than all those other folk. When a person has tamed themselves, always living restrained,

title: All tremble at the rod
situation: A man has power over someone weaker and is deciding how far to use it.
wise_response: The verse says all tremble at punishment and fear death, and asks him to treat others as himself: neither kill nor cause killing.
why_it_worked: It makes the other person's fear the measure, so the question changes from what he can do to what he would accept.
tempting_wrong_answer: Use the power, since the other person cannot stop him.
original_text: Sabbe tasanti daṇḍassa, sabbe bhāyanti maccuno; Attānaṁ upamaṁ katvā, na haneyya na ghātaye.
scholarly_translation: All tremble at the rod, all fear death. Treating others like oneself, neither kill nor incite to kill.

title: The miserly do not praise giving
situation: A man has more than he needs and is deciding whether to keep it.
wise_response: The verse says the miserly do not rise, and only a fool does not praise giving; the attentive celebrate it.
why_it_worked: It treats giving as what a clear-headed person does rather than as a sacrifice, so the decision becomes a question of judgment rather than loss.
tempting_wrong_answer: Hold on to it and call the holding prudence.
original_text: Na ve kadariyā devalokaṁ vajanti, Bālā have nappasaṁsanti dānaṁ; Dhīro ca dānaṁ anumodamāno, Teneva so hoti sukhī parattha.
scholarly_translation: The miserly don't ascend to heaven, it takes a fool to not praise giving. The attentive celebrate giving, and so find happiness in the hereafter.

title: Patient acceptance is the highest fervor
situation: A man is provoked and can end the argument by force.
wise_response: The verse calls patient endurance the highest austerity, and says no renunciate injures another.
why_it_worked: It makes restraint the discipline rather than the fallback, so endurance counts as the achievement and not as losing.
tempting_wrong_answer: Answer force with force and call the restraint weakness.
original_text: Khantī paramaṁ tapo titikkhā, Nibbānaṁ paramaṁ vadanti buddhā; Na hi pabbajito parūpaghātī, Na samaṇo hoti paraṁ viheṭhayanto.
scholarly_translation: Patient acceptance is the ultimate fervor. Extinguishment is the ultimate, say the Buddhas. No true renunciate injures another, nor does an ascetic hurt another.

title: Content among the greedy
situation: A man lives among people who are always acquiring and finds himself restless.
wise_response: The verse says: let us live happily, content among the greedy.
why_it_worked: It separates his measure of a good life from the one the people around him are using.
tempting_wrong_answer: Take their measure as the real one and call his restlessness ambition.
original_text: Susukhaṁ vata jīvāma, ussukesu anussukā; Ussukesu manussesu, viharāma anussukā.
scholarly_translation: Let us live so very happily, content among the greedy. Among greedy humans, let us live content.

title: Checking the chariot
situation: A man feels anger rise and has a moment before he speaks.
wise_response: The verse says to check anger like a charioteer pulling a lurching chariot; that is what makes someone a driver rather than a passenger.
why_it_worked: It puts the test in the first second, where he still has a choice, instead of after the words are out.
tempting_wrong_answer: Let the anger speak and call it honesty.
original_text: Yo ve uppatitaṁ kodhaṁ, rathaṁ bhantaṁva vāraye; Tamahaṁ sārathiṁ brūmi, rasmiggāho itaro jano.
scholarly_translation: When anger surges like a lurching chariot, keep it in check. That's what I call a charioteer; others just hold the reins.

title: Defeat each fault with its opposite
situation: A man is being lied about and belittled by someone who is behaving worse than he is.
wise_response: The verse says to defeat anger with kindness, villainy with virtue, stinginess with giving, and lies with truth.
why_it_worked: It answers each fault with its opposite rather than its equal, so the exchange cannot continue on the other person's terms.
tempting_wrong_answer: Answer each attack in kind and call it standing up for himself.
original_text: Akkodhena jine kodhaṁ, asādhuṁ sādhunā jine; Jine kadariyaṁ dānena, saccenālikavādinaṁ.
scholarly_translation: Defeat anger with kindness, villainy with virtue, stinginess with giving, and lies with truth.
